## Answer to the task

**Tuple class** — annotate with `@TypedTuple`; APT generates `StoreAggregateMapper`. No hand-written mapping, no Lombok:

```java
@TypedTuple
public class StoreAggregate {
    private long storeId;
    private int bookCount;
    private BigDecimal minPrice;
    // plain getters/setters
}
```

The generated mapper has exactly one fluent method per declared component and no separate root entry point — the chain starts with the static method named after the first component (`storeId`). Grouping, ordering and the client stay on the query:

```java
var b = Tables.BOOK_TABLE;
List<StoreAggregate> rows = sqlClient.createQuery(b)
    .groupBy(b.storeId())
    .orderBy(b.storeId().asc())
    .select(
        StoreAggregateMapper
            .storeId(b.storeId())
            .bookCount(Expression.rowCount())
            .minPrice(b.price().min())
    )
    .execute();
```

Java select expressions have no arbitrary `.as("alias")`; the mapper chain is the projection.

**Large result sets** — there is no JDBC `stream()` query API and calling `.execute().stream()` does not give bounded database consumption. Use `forEach`, which processes results in fetch batches and returns only after consumption, so keep the connection/transaction alive for the whole call:

```java
sqlClient.createQuery(b)
    .groupBy(b.storeId())
    .orderBy(b.storeId().asc())
    .select(StoreAggregateMapper
        .storeId(b.storeId())
        .bookCount(Expression.rowCount())
        .minPrice(b.price().min()))
    .forEach(128, row -> { /* consume */ });
```

If the operation needs resumability, use an ID-keyset page loop instead. `forEach`'s batch size limits fetch batches, not a single root's enormous collection.
